findings.detail: The old lane was workflow_dispatch on master. Branch code was only compiled and ad-hoc signed in a secretless job, and publication ran master's reviewed scripts. The new lane triggers on any push to `dev` and calls `./.github/workflows/release-provider.yml` with `secrets: inherit` (head lines 103-106). That reusable workflow is taken from the pushed commit, so whoever can push `dev` controls the workflow, the build action and the scripts. The header comment (lines 30-35) admits `dev` has no pull_request or review rule. A malicious or compromised push could edit the workflow to exfiltrate every repository secret. These include APPLE_CERTIFICATE_P12, APPLE_APP_PASSWORD, and PROD_RELEASE_KEY/STAGING_* values, since the comment says they are all repository secrets with no environment scoping. Branch code also runs in the signing job (for example the smoke test of the signed binary). The result is Developer ID signing and notarization of unreviewed code under the same team ID that the self-updater's production designated requirement accepts (release-provider.yml lines 829-834). It also exposes the prod release key that controls the trusted-binary registry. The check that master's copy of verify-source runs lives inside the attacker-editable workflow, so it does not bind. Fix: require a pull_request/review ruleset on `dev` before enabling the trigger. Bind the signing and prod secrets to protected GitHub environments, so a dev ref cannot read them. Pass explicit DEV_* secrets instead of `secrets: inherit`. Pin the reusable workflow to master with `uses: ...@master`, or a SHA.
findings.title: Unreviewed dev-branch push now runs the pushed workflow with inherited Developer ID, notarization and release secrets
